rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: The colligative property used for the determination of molar mass of polymers and proteins is :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '1. (a)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'Osmotic pressure'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: polymers and proteins have very large molar masses, so even a fairly heavy sample gives very few moles and hence a very dilute solution. The depression in freezing point, the elevation in boiling point and the relative lowering of vapour pressure produced by such a solution are all too small to measure reliably, whereas its osmotic pressure is still large enough to measure — and it is measured at room temperature, so the biomolecule is not destroyed by heating.

rows.stem: Low concentration of oxygen in the blood and tissues of people living at high altitude is due to :

options.label: D
options.text: both low temperature and high atmospheric pressure

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '2. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'low atmospheric pressure'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: by Henry's law the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. At high altitude the total atmospheric pressure is low, so the partial pressure of oxygen is low, so less oxygen dissolves in the blood. The resulting low oxygen level in blood and tissues is called anoxia.

rows.stem:
The correct cell to represent the following reaction is :
\(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\)
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '3. (d)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(\mathrm{Zn} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} \parallel \mathrm{Ag^{+}} \mid \mathrm{Ag}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in a cell representation the anode, where oxidation happens, is written on the left and the cathode, where reduction happens, on the right, with the salt bridge shown as \(\parallel\). In \(\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{Ag^{+}} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}\) zinc is oxidised and silver ion is reduced, so the left half-cell must be \(\mathrm{Zn} \mid \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) and the right half-cell \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}} \mid \mathrm{Ag}\), each written with the species in contact with the electrode first.

rows.stem: \(\Delta \mathrm{G}\) and \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\) for a spontaneous reaction will be :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '4. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'negative, positive'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two quantities are linked by \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -\,n F E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\). A spontaneous reaction has \(\Delta G\) negative, and since \(n\) and \(F\) are both positive, that requires \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\) to be positive.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: Which of the following is affected by catalyst ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '5. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(\mathrm{E_a}\), the activation energy.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: a catalyst works by providing an alternative path with a lower activation energy, so more molecules have enough energy to react and the reaction speeds up. \(\Delta H\), \(\Delta G\) and \(\Delta S\) depend only on the initial and final states, which the catalyst does not change — which is also why a catalyst can never make a non-spontaneous reaction happen.

rows.stem:
The order of the reaction
\(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2\,(g)} \xrightarrow{\ h\nu\ } 2\mathrm{HCl\,(g)}\) is :
rows.solution:
CBSE WITHDREW this question. Its marking-scheme entry reads '(c) / Full mark to be awarded for any option', so every candidate was given the mark whatever they marked, and the printed letter is not a key to rely on. The scheme states no reason for the withdrawal.

For reference, the letter CBSE printed is (c), i.e. the option '0'. The photochemical combination of hydrogen and chlorine, \(\mathrm{H_2\,(g)} + \mathrm{Cl_2\,(g)} \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\mathrm{HCl\,(g)}\), is the standard textbook example of a zero-order reaction: the rate is fixed by the intensity of the light absorbed rather than by how much hydrogen or chlorine is present, so rate \(= k[\mathrm{H_2}]^{0}[\mathrm{Cl_2}]^{0} = k\).

rows.stem: The most common and stable oxidation state of a Lanthanoid is :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '7. (b)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(+\,3\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the lanthanoids have the configuration \(\mathrm{[Xe]}\,4f^{n}\,5d^{0-1}\,6s^{2}\). Loss of the two \(6s\) electrons together with one more electron gives \(\mathrm{Ln^{3+}}\), and it is the \(+3\) ion that is stable right across the series. The occasional \(+2\) and \(+4\) states appear only where they leave an empty, half-filled or completely filled \(4f\) sub-shell.

rows.stem: The compounds \(\mathrm{[Co(SO_4)\,(NH_3)_5]\,Br}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(Br)\,(NH_3)_5]\,SO_4}\) represent :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '8. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'ionisation isomerism'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the two compounds have the same composition but exchange the ion held inside the coordination sphere with the counter ion outside it. \(\mathrm{[Co(SO_4)(NH_3)_5]Br}\) releases \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) in solution, while \(\mathrm{[Co(Br)(NH_3)_5]SO_4}\) releases \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\). Isomers that differ in this way, and therefore give different ions on dissolving, are ionisation isomers.

rows.stem: The synthesis of alkyl fluoride is best obtained from :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '9. (b)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'Swartz reaction'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in the Swartz reaction an alkyl chloride or bromide is heated with a metallic fluoride such as \(\mathrm{AgF}\), \(\mathrm{Hg_2F_2}\), \(\mathrm{CoF_2}\) or \(\mathrm{SbF_3}\), and halogen exchange gives the alkyl fluoride. Direct fluorination is too violent to control; the Finkelstein reaction, with \(\mathrm{NaI}\) in dry acetone, makes iodides; and the Sandmeyer reaction makes aryl halides from a diazonium salt, not alkyl halides.

rows.stem: In the reaction \(\mathrm{R-OH} + \mathrm{HCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ZnCl_2}} \mathrm{RCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\), what is the correct order of reactivity of alcohol ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '10. (a)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(1^{\circ} < 2^{\circ} < 3^{\circ}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in this reaction the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) is first protonated and then leaves as water, giving a carbocation. A tertiary carbocation is the most stable of the three and forms most readily, so a tertiary alcohol reacts fastest and a primary alcohol slowest — which is exactly what the Lucas test uses to tell the three classes apart.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\) on reaction with NaOH and \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) in alcoholic medium gives :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '11. (b)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\).

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: an amide treated with bromine and alkali undergoes the Hofmann bromamide degradation, \(\mathrm{RCONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RNH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\). The primary amine produced has ONE CARBON FEWER than the amide, because the carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate, so \(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\) gives methanamine and not ethanamine.

rows.stem: Which of the following is least basic ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '12. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is \(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the basicity of an amine depends on how available its nitrogen lone pair is. In aniline that lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance, so it is much less available for donation. In ammonia the lone pair is free, and in the methylamines the alkyl groups push electron density towards nitrogen, making them more basic still. Aniline is therefore the weakest base of the four.

rows.stem: The glycosidic linkage involved in linking the glucose units in amylase part of starch is :
rows.solution:
CBSE WITHDREW this question. Its marking-scheme entry reads '(c) / Award full mark if attempted (Printing error)', so the mark was given to every candidate who attempted it, and the printed letter is not a key to rely on.

The printing error is in the stem itself: the paper prints 'amylase', which is the starch-digesting ENZYME, where 'amylose' — the unbranched fraction of starch — is meant. As printed, the question asks about the glycosidic linkage in an enzyme, which has none.

For reference, the letter CBSE printed is (c), i.e. the option \(\mathrm{C_1 - C_4}\ \alpha\) linkage. In amylose the glucose units are joined head to tail by \(\mathrm{C_1 - C_4}\) glycosidic linkages of \(\alpha\) configuration; the \(\mathrm{C_1 - C_6}\) \(\alpha\) linkage is the one that creates the branch points in the other fraction of starch, amylopectin.

rows.stem: An \(\alpha\)-helix is a structural feature of :
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '14. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is 'Polypeptides'.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the \(\alpha\)-helix is one of the two common secondary structures of proteins. It forms when a polypeptide chain coils into a right-handed spiral held in place by hydrogen bonds between the \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) of one peptide unit and the \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) of the fourth unit along the chain. Sucrose and starch are carbohydrates and nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids, so none of them can show this feature.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group is o- and p-directing in electrophilic substitution reactions.
Reason (R) : Aniline cannot undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '15. (b)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is that both statements are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the Assertion is true — the nitrogen lone pair of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group is delocalised into the ring, and the resonance structures put the extra electron density at the ortho and para positions, so the group is activating and o-, p-directing. The Reason is also true, but it holds for a quite different cause: aniline's lone pair binds to the Lewis acid \(\mathrm{AlCl_3}\), and the resulting salt has a positively charged nitrogen that strongly deactivates the ring, so Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation both fail. Since the failure of the Friedel-Crafts reaction says nothing about WHERE an electrophile attacks, the Reason does not explain the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Acetylation of aniline gives a monosubstituted product.
Reason (R) : Activating effect of \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\) group is more than that of amino group.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '16. (c)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is that the Assertion is true but the Reason is false.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: acetylation of aniline with acetic anhydride or acetyl chloride does stop at the monosubstituted product, acetanilide, so the Assertion is true. The Reason inverts the actual cause. Once the \(\mathrm{-COCH_3}\) group is attached, the nitrogen lone pair is drawn towards its carbonyl group and is much less available, so the \(\mathrm{-NHCOCH_3}\) group is LESS activating than \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\), not more — and it is precisely that reduced activation which stops a second substitution.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The molecularity of the reaction \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HBr}\) appears to be 2.
Reason (R) : Two molecules of the reactants are involved in the given elementary reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '17. (a)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is that both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: molecularity is the number of species that must come together in a single step for a reaction to occur. The equation \(\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{HBr}\) shows two molecules on the left, so read as a single step it looks bimolecular — which is why the Assertion is worded 'appears to be'.

Worth knowing: this is the standard textbook example of a reaction whose order is NOT its apparent molecularity. Experimentally rate \(= k[\mathrm{H_2}][\mathrm{Br_2}]^{1/2}\), an order of \(3/2\), because the reaction actually proceeds through a chain of steps rather than in one.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Low spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed.
Reason (R) : Crystal field splitting energy is less than pairing energy for tetrahedral complexes.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme answers Section A with the option letter alone: its table reads '18. (a)', and no justification is printed.

The keyed option is that both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in a tetrahedral field only four ligands approach the metal, and they approach between the axes rather than along them, so the crystal field splitting is small — \(\Delta_t = \tfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o\) for the same metal and ligands. It is therefore almost always smaller than the energy needed to force two electrons into one orbital, so the electrons stay unpaired and the complex is high spin. Low-spin tetrahedral complexes are correspondingly rare.

rows.stem: What is Henry's law ? Give one application of it.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

Henry's law states that the partial vapour pressure of a gas is directly proportional to the mole fraction of the gas in the solution, \(p = \mathrm{K_H}\,x\), where \(p\) is the partial pressure of the gas, \(x\) is its mole fraction in solution and \(\mathrm{K_H}\) is Henry's constant.

Application (the scheme accepts ANY ONE of these, or any other correct application):

- To increase the solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in soft drinks and soda water, the bottle is sealed under high pressure.
- To minimize the painful effects accompanying the decompression of deep-sea divers (bends), oxygen diluted with less soluble helium gas is used for breathing.
- At higher altitudes, low blood oxygen causes climbers to become weak and unable to think clearly (anoxia).

rows.stem: On diluting two electrolytes 'A' and 'B', the \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) of 'A' increases 25 times while that of 'B' increases by \(1{\cdot}5\) times. Which of the two electrolytes is strong ? Justify your answer graphically.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

'B' is a strong electrolyte.

The justification the scheme prints is a graph, not prose. It plots \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) on the vertical axis against \(c^{1/2}\) on the horizontal axis and carries two curves: one labelled 'A (Weak electrolyte)', which rises almost vertically as \(c^{1/2}\) approaches zero and then falls away very steeply, and one labelled 'B (Strong Electrolyte)', which is very nearly a straight line of small negative slope.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme, so that the graph can be read: for a strong electrolyte the ions are already fully formed, so diluting the solution only lets them move further apart and \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) rises very little; the plot against \(c^{1/2}\) is close to linear and can be extrapolated to \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\). For a weak electrolyte the degree of dissociation itself climbs steeply on dilution, so \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) increases enormously near infinite dilution and the curve cannot be extrapolated. A 25-fold increase on dilution therefore marks 'A' as the weak electrolyte, and the \(1{\cdot}5\)-fold increase marks 'B' as the strong one.

rows.stem: The electrical resistance of a column of \(0{\cdot}05\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) NaOH solution of diameter 1 cm and length 50 cm is \(5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{3}\) ohm. Calculate the conductivity.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

\(A = \pi r^{2} = 3{\cdot}14 \times (0{\cdot}5)^{2} = 0{\cdot}785\ \mathrm{cm^{2}}\), \(\ell = 50\ \mathrm{cm}\)

\(k = \dfrac{\ell}{R \times A}\)

\(= \dfrac{50}{0{\cdot}785 \times (5{\cdot}55 \times 10^{3})}\)

\(= 11{\cdot}47 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}}\)

(or by any other correct method)

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the \(0{\cdot}5\ \mathrm{cm}\) is the radius, half of the stated 1 cm diameter, and the cell constant used is \(\ell / A = 50 / 0{\cdot}785 = 63{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete the following equations :
(a) \(2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 5\mathrm{NO_2^{-}} + 6\mathrm{H}^{+} \longrightarrow\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H}^{+} + 6\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow\)
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) \(2\mathrm{MnO_4^{-}} + 5\mathrm{NO_2^{-}} + 6\mathrm{H^{+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{NO_3^{-}} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^{+}} + 6\mathrm{e^{-}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.stem:
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCl_5}} \text{'A'} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{AgCN}} \text{'B'}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2Cl} + \mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\text{ethanol}} \text{'A'} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HBr}} \text{'B'}\)
Identify 'A' and 'B' in the above reactions.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme (the scheme prints each compound as a drawn structure and gives the name beside it):

(a) A is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(Cl)-CH_3}\), 2-chloropropane.
B is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(NC)-CH_3}\), isopropyl isocyanide / propan-2-isonitrile.

(b) A is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH_2}\), propene.
B is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(Br)-CH_3}\), 2-bromopropane.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: in (a) \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) replaces the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) of propan-2-ol by \(\mathrm{-Cl}\), and \(\mathrm{AgCN}\) — being largely covalent, so that only the nitrogen lone pair is free to attack — gives the ISOcyanide rather than the cyanide. In (b) alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) eliminates \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to give propene, and \(\mathrm{HBr}\) then adds by Markovnikov's rule, putting the bromine on the middle carbon.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(i) Phenol is a stronger acid than an alcohol.
(ii) The boiling point of alcohols decreases with increase in branching of alkyl chain.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Because phenoxide ion is more stable due to resonance than alkoxide ion. (or any other correct explanation)

(ii) Because branching decreases the surface area / the van der Waals force decreases with a decrease in surface area.

rows.stem:
(i) Write the mechanism of the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[443\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{H}^{+}} \mathrm{CH_2 = CH_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
(ii) Write the equation involved in Reimer-Tiemann reaction.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) The mechanism is printed as three drawn steps, with curved arrows showing the movement of each electron pair; the scheme awards the marks for ANY TWO CORRECT STEPS.

Step 1 (fast): the oxygen of ethanol is protonated —
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H^{+}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH_2^{+}}\)

Step 2 (slow): the protonated alcohol loses water, giving the ethyl carbocation —
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH_2^{+}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2^{+}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3: a proton is lost from the adjacent carbon, giving the alkene —
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2^{+}} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^{+}}\)

(ii) Reimer-Tiemann reaction. The scheme prints it twice. In full: phenol treated with \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) gives the sodium salt of o-hydroxybenzal chloride — the ring carrying \(\mathrm{-O^{-}Na^{+}}\) and \(\mathrm{-CHCl_2}\) on adjacent carbons — which \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) hydrolyses to the sodium salt of salicylaldehyde, and \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) then converts to salicylaldehyde. Condensed: phenol, treated with (i) \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and aqueous \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) and then (ii) \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), gives salicylaldehyde, i.e. 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde.

rows.stem:
Explain briefly :
(a) Carbylamine reaction
(b) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme (in each part an explanation OR the reaction earns the mark):

(a) Carbylamine reaction — aliphatic and aromatic primary amines on heating with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide form isocyanides, or carbylamines, which are foul-smelling substances:
\(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Isocyanide with an offensive smell is formed.

(b) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis — phthalimide on treatment with ethanolic potassium hydroxide forms potassium salt of phthalimide, which on heating with alkyl halide followed by alkaline hydrolysis produces the corresponding primary amine.

The scheme also draws the whole sequence in structures: phthalimide \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{KOH}}\) potassium phthalimide \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{R-X}}\) N-alkylphthalimide \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}}\) the primary amine \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\) together with the disodium salt of phthalic acid.

rows.stem:
(a) Write chemical reaction to show that open structure of D-glucose contains the straight chain.
(b) What type of linkage is responsible for the formation of protein ?
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) Glucose on prolonged heating with \(\mathrm{HI}\) gives n-hexane, which shows that all six carbon atoms are joined in a straight chain:
\(\mathrm{CHO-(CHOH)_4-CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HI},\ \Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3}\) (n-Hexane)

(b) Peptide linkage.

rows.stem:
(a) Differentiate between Ideal solution and Non-ideal solution.
(b) 30 g of urea is dissolved in 846 g of water. Calculate the vapour pressure of water for this solution if vapour pressure of pure water at 298 K is \(23{\cdot}8\) mm Hg.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) Any one difference, or any other correct difference:

| Ideal Solution | Non-ideal solution |
|---|---|
| The solution obeys Raoult's law at all concentrations. | The solution does not obey Raoult's law. |
| \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{mixing}} = 0\) and \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{mixing}} = 0\) | \(\Delta V_{\mathrm{mixing}} \neq 0\) and \(\Delta H_{\mathrm{mixing}} \neq 0\) |

(b) \(\dfrac{\mathrm{P_A^{\circ}} - \mathrm{P_A}}{\mathrm{P_A^{\circ}}} = \dfrac{w_B / M_B}{(w_B / M_B) + (w_A / M_A)}\)

The scheme then works it two ways and reaches the same value by both.

First: \(1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{P_A}}{23{\cdot}8} = \dfrac{30/60}{846/18}\), so \(\mathrm{P_A} = \dfrac{46{\cdot}5}{47} \times 23{\cdot}8 = 23{\cdot}5\) mm Hg.

Or: \(1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{P_A}}{23{\cdot}8} = \dfrac{30/60}{\dfrac{846}{18} + \dfrac{30}{60}}\), so \(\mathrm{P_A} = \dfrac{47}{47{\cdot}5} \times 23{\cdot}8 = 23{\cdot}5\) mm Hg.

(Full marks may be awarded if the student substitutes \(\mathrm{M_B}\) for molar mass as the molar mass of urea is not given in the question.)

A note on the QUESTION, not on the scheme: the paper does not supply the molar mass of urea, so as printed the arithmetic cannot be completed from the data given. The scheme takes \(\mathrm{M_B} = 60\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\) and says so itself in the bracket above.

rows.stem:
Write main product formed when :
(a) Methyl chloride is treated with NaI/Acetone.
(b) 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene is subjected to hydrolysis.
(c) n-Butyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3I}\) / Iodomethane / Methyl iodide

(b) Picric acid / 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol / 2,4,6-Trinitrobenzenol. The scheme prints the structure: a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\), with \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) groups at the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

(c) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2}\) / But-1-ene

rows.stem:
How do you convert the following : (Any three)
(a) Phenol to picric acid
(b) Propanone to 2-Methylpropan-2-ol
(c) Phenol to anisole
(d) Propene to Propan-1-ol
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme prints all four conversions, of which the question asks for any three; each is followed by 'or by any other correct method'. The scheme draws the aromatic compounds as ring structures.

(a) Phenol to picric acid: phenol with concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, i.e. picric acid — the ring keeping its \(\mathrm{-OH}\) and gaining \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) at the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

(b) Propanone to 2-methylpropan-2-ol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)}\ \mathrm{H_2O}/\mathrm{H^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)}\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-OH}\)

(c) Phenol to anisole:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CH_3I}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OCH_3}\)

(d) Propene to propan-1-ol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)}\ \mathrm{NaOH-H_2O_2}]{\mathrm{(i)}\ \mathrm{(H-BH_2)_2}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-OH}\)

rows.stem:
Explain why :
(i) Carboxyl group in benzoic acid is meta directing.
(ii) Sodium bisulphite is used for the purification of aldehydes and ketones.
(iii) Carboxylic acids do not give characteristic reactions of carbonyl group.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Because it is an electron-withdrawing group / deactivating group / \(-\mathrm{R}\) effect, electrophilic substitution takes place at the m-position.

(ii) Because aldehydes and ketones form an addition compound with \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\) which on hydrolysis forms pure aldehydes and ketones.

(iii) Due to resonance, the carboxylic carbon becomes less electrophilic.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: An organic compound 'A', having the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_8O}\) on treatment with Cu at 573 K, gives 'B'. 'B' does not reduce Fehling's solution but gives a yellow precipitate of the compound 'C' with \(\mathrm{I_2/NaOH}\). Deduce the structures of A, B and C.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme (or an explanation with the correct structures of A, B and C):

\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu},\ 573\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{Heat}]{\mathrm{NaOH}/\mathrm{I_2}} \mathrm{CHI_3}\)

So A is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH(OH)-CH_3}\), propan-2-ol; B is \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\), propanone; and C is \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\), iodoform.

rows.stem:
(a) What are the hydrolysis products of (i) Lactose, (ii) Maltose ?
(b) Give the basic structural difference between starch and cellulose.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(a) (i) Glucose and Galactose.  (ii) Glucose and Glucose.

(b) Starch is a polymer of \(\alpha\)-glucose while cellulose is a polymer of \(\beta\)-glucose. (or any other correct structural difference)

rows.stem: What is average rate of reaction ?
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme: change in the concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme, because the printed value point is very compressed: what makes a rate an AVERAGE rate is that the change is measured over a finite interval of time rather than at one instant. For \(\mathrm{R} \longrightarrow \mathrm{P}\),
\(r_{\mathrm{av}} = -\,\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{R}]}{\Delta t} = +\,\dfrac{\Delta[\mathrm{P}]}{\Delta t}\)
the minus sign keeping the rate positive even though the reactant concentration is falling.

Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution: CBSE's marking scheme: concentration of reactants, surface area, catalyst and temperature. (any two)

rows.stem:
(1) What happens to rate of reaction for zero order reaction ?
(2) What is the unit of k for zero order reaction ?
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(1) Rate is independent of the concentration of reactant(s) / rate remains constant / rate \(= k\).

(2) \(\mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\)

rows.stem:
(1) For a reaction \(\mathrm{P} + 2\mathrm{Q} \longrightarrow \text{Products}\)
Rate \(= \mathrm{k[P]}^{1/2}\,\mathrm{[Q]}^{1}\). What is the order of the reaction ?
(2) Define pseudo first order reaction with an example.
rows.context: The rate of reaction is concerned with decrease in concentration of reactants or increase in the concentration of products per unit time. It can be expressed as instantaneous rate at a particular instant of time and average rate over a large interval of time. Mathematical representation of rate of reaction is given by rate law. Rate constant and order of a reaction can be determined from rate law or its integrated rate equation.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(1) \(3/2\) / \(1{\cdot}5\)

(2) A reaction that appears to be of higher order but follows first-order kinetics. Example: hydrolysis of an ester. (or any other correct example)

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the order in (1) is simply the sum of the exponents in the rate law, \(\tfrac{1}{2} + 1 = \tfrac{3}{2}\).

rows.stem: If \(\mathrm{PtCl_2 \cdot 2NH_3}\) does not react with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\), what will be its formula ?
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme: \(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]}\)

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: no reaction with \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) means no chloride ion is free in the solution, so both chlorides must lie inside the coordination sphere — satisfying secondary valency rather than primary valency — and the complex is therefore neutral, with no ion outside the square brackets.

rows.stem: What is the secondary valency of \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]^{3+}}\) ?
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme: 6

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: 'en' is ethane-1,2-diamine, a bidentate ligand, so each of the three occupies two coordination positions. The secondary valency is the coordination number, which is therefore \(3 \times 2 = 6\).

rows.stem:
Write the hybridization and magnetic behaviour of \(\mathrm{[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}}\).
[Atomic number : Ni = 28]
rows.context: In coordination compounds, metals show two types of linkages, primary and secondary. Primary valencies are ionisable and are satisfied by negatively charged ions. Secondary valencies are non-ionisable and are satisfied by neutral or negative ions having lone pair of electrons. Primary valencies are non-directional while secondary valencies decide the shape of the complexes.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme: \(\mathrm{dsp^2}\), diamagnetic.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{8}\). Cyanide is a strong-field ligand, so the two unpaired \(3d\) electrons pair up and one \(3d\) orbital is left empty. That orbital, together with the \(4s\) and two of the \(4p\) orbitals, gives \(\mathrm{dsp^2}\) hybridisation and a square planar shape, and since no unpaired electron is left the complex is diamagnetic.

rows.stem:
(i) State Kohlrausch's law of independent migration of ions. Write an expression for the limiting molar conductivity of acetic acid according to Kohlrausch's law.
(ii) Calculate the maximum work and \(\log \mathrm{K_c}\) for the given reaction at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Ni\,(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag}^{+}\,\mathrm{(aq)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ni}^{2+}\,\mathrm{(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag\,(s)}\)
Given : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}/\mathrm{Ni}} = -\,0{\cdot}25\) V, \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag}^{+}/\mathrm{Ag}} = +\,0{\cdot}80\) V
1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte can be represented as the sum of the individual contributions of the anion and cation of the electrolyte:
\(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{CH_3COO^{-}}) + \lambda^{\circ}(\mathrm{H^{+}})\)

(ii) \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -\,n F E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\)

Maximum work \(= -\,\Delta_r G^{\circ} = n F E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}\)

\(= 2 \times 96500\ \mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}} \times (0{\cdot}80 + 0{\cdot}25)\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= 2 \times 96500 \times 1{\cdot}05\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\)

\(= 202{,}650\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}\), or \(202{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\)

\(\log \mathrm{K_c} = \dfrac{n E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}}}{0{\cdot}059} = \dfrac{2 \times 1{\cdot}05}{0{\cdot}059} = 35{\cdot}6\)

rows.stem:
(i) State Faraday's first law of electrolysis. How much charge, in terms of Faraday, is required for the reduction of 1 mol \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\) to Cu ?
(ii) Calculate emf of the following cell at 298 K for
\(\mathrm{Mg\,(s)} \mid \mathrm{Mg}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}1\ \mathrm{M}) \parallel \mathrm{Cu}^{2+}\,(0{\cdot}01\ \mathrm{M}) \mid \mathrm{Cu\,(s)}\)
[\(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{cell}} = +\,2{\cdot}71\) V, 1 F = 96500 C \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), \(\log 10 = 1\)]
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) It states that the mass of a substance deposited or liberated at the electrodes is directly proportional to the charge, or quantity of electricity, passed through the electrolyte.
2F charge is required.

(ii) \(\mathrm{E_{cell}} = \mathrm{E^{\circ}_{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}0591}{2} \log \dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}\)

\(= 2{\cdot}71\ \mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}0591}{2} \log \dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{0{\cdot}01}\)

\(= 2{\cdot}71\ \mathrm{V} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}0591}{2} \log 10\)

\(= 2{\cdot}71\ \mathrm{V} - 0{\cdot}0295\)

\(= 2{\cdot}68\ \mathrm{V}\)

(Deduct \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) mark for no or incorrect unit.)

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assign reason for each of the following :
(i) Manganese exhibits the highest oxidation state of +7 among the 3d series of transition elements.
(ii) Transition metals and their compounds are generally found to be good catalysts in chemical reactions.
(iii) \(\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}\) is reducing in nature while with the same d-orbital configuration \((\mathrm{d}^{4})\) \(\mathrm{Mn}^{3+}\) is an oxidising agent.
(iv) Zn has lowest enthalpy of atomization.
(v) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{+}\) is unstable in an aqueous solution.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) Due to the participation of all \(3d\) and \(4s\) electrons in bond formation / due to the presence of the maximum number of unpaired electrons.

(ii) Due to variable oxidation state / due to the ability to adopt multiple oxidation states / due to the large surface area / due to complex formation.

(iii) \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\) changes from \(d^{4}\) to the stable half-filled \(t_{2g}^{3}\) configuration, while \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) changes to the stable half-filled \(d^{5}\) configuration.

(iv) Due to the absence of unpaired electrons and weak interatomic interactions.

(v) \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) ion (aq.) undergoes disproportionation to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) (aq.) and Cu:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\,\mathrm{(aq.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\,\mathrm{(aq.)} + \mathrm{Cu\,(s)}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Carry out the following conversions :
(1) Ethanal to But-2-en-1-al
(2) Propanoic acid to 2-chloropropanoic acid
(ii) An alkene with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_5H_{10}}\) on ozonolysis gives a mixture of two compounds 'B' and 'C'. Compound 'B' gives positive Fehling test and also reacts with iodine and NaOH solution. Compound 'C' does not give Fehling solution test but forms iodoform. Identify the compounds 'A', 'B' and 'C'.
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) (1) Ethanal to but-2-en-1-al, by aldol condensation followed by loss of water on heating:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)-CH_2-CHO} \xrightarrow[-\,\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}CH-CHO}\)

(2) Propanoic acid to 2-chloropropanoic acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-COOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)}\ \mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{(i)}\ \mathrm{Cl_2}/\text{Red P}} \mathrm{CH_3-CH(Cl)-COOH}\)

(ii) The scheme prints each compound as a drawn structure with the name beside it:

A is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}C(CH_3)-CH_3}\) / 2-Methylbut-2-ene
B is \(\mathrm{H_3C-CHO}\) / Ethanal / Acetaldehyde
C is \(\mathrm{CH_3-CO-CH_3}\) / Propanone / Acetone

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Distinguish with a suitable chemical test :
(1) \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_2CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CHO}\)
(2) Ethanal and Ethanoic acid
(ii) Write the structure of oxime of acetone.
(iii) Identify A to D.
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{PCl_5}} \mathrm{A} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2/Pd-BaSO_4}} \mathrm{B} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H_3O^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ CH_3/MgBr}} \mathrm{C}\)
and \(\mathrm{B} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LiAlH_4}} \mathrm{D}\)
rows.solution:
CBSE's marking scheme:

(i) (1) Add iodine \((\mathrm{I_2})\), \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), and heat both the test tubes containing the given organic compounds. Butanone gives a yellow precipitate \((\mathrm{CHI_3})\) while butanal will not give the positive iodoform test.

(2) Add \(\mathrm{NaHCO_3}\) in both the test tubes containing the given organic compounds. Ethanoic acid will give brisk effervescence of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and ethanal will not.

(or any other suitable chemical test)

(ii) The scheme's answer here is a drawn structure: the oxime of acetone, with two methyl groups on a carbon that is doubly bonded to nitrogen and the nitrogen carrying \(\mathrm{-OH}\) — that is, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}N-OH}\).

(iii) A is \(\mathrm{CH_3COCl}\), B is \(\mathrm{CH_3CHO}\), C is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH(OH)}\) and D is \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH}\).

A note on the QUESTION, not on the scheme: the paper prints the Grignard reagent in that sequence as 'CH3/MgBr'. The scheme reads it as \(\mathrm{CH_3MgBr}\), which is what makes C propan-2-ol.
